title: Compare thirds, fourths and fifths
context: Same lower note: C4 · equal temperament · A4 = 440 Hz
caption: From C4: Eb4 makes a minor third (3 semitones), E4 a major third (4), F4 a perfect fourth (5), G4 a perfect fifth (7), and C5 an octave (12). These are synthetic references, not identified choir parts.

pairs.label: Minor third
pairs.comment: C4–Eb4 spans three semitones. Eb is the correct spelling for this third, rather than D#.

pairs.label: Major third
pairs.comment: C4–E4 spans four semitones: one chromatic step wider than the minor third.

pairs.label: Perfect fourth
pairs.comment: C4–F4 spans five semitones. Compare its width with the thirds, then audition the separate reference audio.

pairs.label: Perfect fifth
pairs.comment: C4–G4 spans seven semitones. In recorded vocals, check two fundamentals; a harmonic peak alone is not a second singer.

pairs.label: Octave
pairs.comment: C4–C5 spans twelve semitones and doubles frequency. The notes share a pitch class but have different registers.

actions.label: Ask agent: compare the two thirds
actions.prompt: Explain the difference between the synthetic reference intervals C4–Eb4 and C4–E4: spelling, 3 versus 4 semitones, and why a third above a melody need not be a constant four-semitone shift. Answer in the conversation language. Do not start a new recording analysis.
